chunks: And As-Sakuni narrated from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said:

A group of people were drinking and became intoxicated, so they began to attack each other with knives they had with them. They were brought before the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), and he imprisoned them. Two of them died, and two remained alive. The families of the two killed men said: 'O Commander of the Faithful! Retaliate against these two for our two relatives.' Imam Ali (peace be upon him) asked the group: 'What do you think?' They replied: 'We think you should retaliate against them.' Imam Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'Perhaps those two who died killed each other.' They said: 'We do not know.' Imam Ali (peace be upon him) then said: 'Rather, I will distribute the blood money of the two killed among the four tribes, and I will deduct the compensation for the injuries of the survivors from the blood money of the deceased.'
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali determine blood money when the specific killer was unknown among a group?
ai.summary: This narration from Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih illustrates Imam Ali’s (as) judicial flexibility in applying diyyah (blood money) when the specific perpetrator within a group is unknown, prioritizing equitable compensation over strict qisas (retaliation). By distributing the deceased's diyyah among the four tribes and using it to cover the survivors' injuries, he demonstrated a pragmatic approach to collective responsibility that balances justice with mercy. This case is frequently cited by Shia jurists to support the principle of 'sabr' (patience/holding back) in qisas when doubt exists regarding the exact killer.
